questions.question_text: A Wyoming broker receives earnest money on Friday afternoon. By when must it be deposited?
distractors: Within 48 hours of receipt
Within 3 business days
By the following Friday
questions.explanation: Wyoming requires trust funds to be deposited no later than the first banking day after receipt. If received Friday afternoon, the deposit must be made by Monday (assuming Monday is a banking day). This is stricter than most states' deposit timelines.

questions.question_text: Where must a Wyoming broker maintain a trust account?
distractors: In any FDIC-insured bank nationwide
In a bank approved by the seller
At the title company handling the closing
questions.explanation: W.S. 33-28-122(a)(i) requires the trust or escrow account to be maintained in a financial institution *in this state*, designated by the word 'trust' or 'escrow' and held in the responsible broker's name (WREC Rules Ch. 5 § 1(a), (c)). The same statute lets a broker use a Wyoming funds holder in lieu of holding the account himself. Out-of-state institutions do not satisfy the requirement, and a nonresident Wyoming licensee must still use a Wyoming funds holder or Wyoming depository (Ch. 5 § 1(h)).

questions.question_text: Which of the following qualifies as trust funds requiring deposit in Wyoming?
questions.correct_answer: Advance listing fees from a seller
distractors: The broker's personal commission check
Office supply reimbursements
A licensee's continuing education fees
questions.explanation: Trust funds include earnest money, down payments, and advance listing fees — any money received on behalf of others in a real estate transaction. A broker's personal commission, office expenses, and education fees are not trust funds.

questions.question_text: Both buyer and seller agree in writing to delay the earnest money deposit by one week. Is this permissible?
questions.correct_answer: Yes, all parties may agree in writing to delay
distractors: No, the first-banking-day rule has no exceptions
Only if WREC grants a written waiver
Yes, but only for deposits under $1,000
questions.explanation: While the default rule requires deposit by the first banking day after receipt, all parties may agree otherwise in writing. This exception allows flexibility when circumstances warrant a delayed deposit, provided every party consents in writing.

questions.question_text: Who must be a signatory on a Wyoming real estate trust account?
distractors: Any licensed agent in the office
The office manager regardless of license
Both the buyer and seller
questions.explanation: WREC Rules Ch. 5 § 1(e)(ii) requires that the responsible broker be able to withdraw money from the trust or escrow account without the benefit of a cosigner — so the responsible broker must have signature authority, and the account is maintained in his name (Ch. 5 § 1(a)). The rule also allows other authorized signatures of licensed *or unlicensed* people to appear on the account, but no one else is required to sign.

questions.question_text: A broker places personal funds in the trust account to cover a business expense. What violation occurred?
questions.correct_answer: Commingling of personal and trust funds
distractors: No violation if the amount is repaid promptly
A bookkeeping error requiring correction only
An accounting violation by the bank
questions.explanation: Commingling the money of others with the broker's own is a disciplinary ground under W.S. 33-28-111(a)(xiv), and W.S. 33-28-122(e) bars commingling trust funds with personal funds. The only carve-out is narrow: funds the broker deposits when establishing the account to keep it open or avoid minimum-balance charges, identified as his own at the time of deposit. Depositing personal funds to cover a business expense fits no exception, and the statute separately forbids using trust deposits for any purpose other than the transaction for which they were provided.

questions.question_text: A broker keeps $50 of personal funds in the trust account to meet the bank's minimum balance. Is this permitted?
questions.correct_answer: Yes, if identified as the broker's own funds at the time of deposit
distractors: No, zero personal funds are ever permitted
Only if WREC approves the balance annually
Yes, but never more than $500
questions.explanation: W.S. 33-28-122(e) provides that it is not commingling if, when establishing the trust account, the responsible broker deposits some of his funds to keep the account open or to avoid charges for a minimum balance, so long as that deposit is identified at the time of deposit. Wyoming sets no dollar cap on that balance — the controls are the permitted purpose and identification at the time of deposit. No other personal funds may be placed in the account.

questions.question_text: A transaction falls through and the buyer wants the earnest money returned. The listing agent claims a share as compensation. When can the agent take compensation from earnest money?
questions.correct_answer: After the transaction is consummated or terminated
distractors: Immediately upon the buyer's cancellation notice
When the broker authorizes the disbursement
At any time per the listing agreement terms
questions.explanation: A licensee is not entitled to compensation from earnest money until the transaction is consummated or terminated according to the contract terms. The agent cannot unilaterally claim a share from earnest money while the outcome is still being resolved.

questions.question_text: A broker deposits a $5,000 commission check into the trust account temporarily. What rule was broken?
distractors: The first-banking-day deposit rule
The signatory requirement
No rule, commissions may pass through trust
questions.explanation: WREC Rules Ch. 5 § 1(a) requires the trust account to be kept separate from personal or business money belonging to the responsible broker, and commingling the money of others with his own is a disciplinary ground under W.S. 33-28-111(a)(xiv). Depositing an outside commission check into trust mixes the broker's money with client funds and is commingling. That is different from money already in trust that becomes due and payable to the broker at closing — Ch. 5 § 1(e)(iv) requires that money to be withdrawn promptly.

questions.question_text: A transaction closes and the responsible broker's commission, held in the firm's trust account, is now earned. What does the WREC rule require?
questions.correct_answer: The broker must withdraw the earned money from the trust account promptly
distractors: The money must remain in trust until the next monthly reconciliation
An affiliated licensee may be paid his split directly from the trust account
WREC must approve the disbursement before it is made
questions.explanation: WREC Rules Ch. 5 § 1(e)(iv) provides that money held in a trust or escrow account which is due and payable to the responsible broker shall be withdrawn promptly — leaving earned funds in trust is itself a violation. The same subsection bars paying monies earned by affiliated licensees directly from the trust or escrow account; the responsible broker must move the money out first and then pay the licensee. Under W.S. 33-28-122(d) nothing is due to a licensee until the transaction is consummated or terminated.

questions.question_text: The buyer and seller dispute who is entitled to the $10,000 earnest money. What should the broker do first?
questions.correct_answer: Continue to hold the deposit in the trust account
distractors: Split the funds equally between the parties
Return the funds to the buyer immediately
Notify WREC and wait for the Commission to decide
questions.explanation: W.S. 33-28-122(f) requires the responsible broker to continue holding a disputed deposit in the trust account until he has a written release from the parties consenting to its disposition, until a civil action is filed, or until he interpleads all parties, at which time the money may be paid to the court. The broker may not pick a side or split the difference, and Wyoming imposes no duty to notify WREC of a dispute — the Commission does not adjudicate earnest money claims.

questions.question_text: What does it mean for a broker to interplead disputed trust funds?
questions.correct_answer: Deposit the funds with the court
distractors: Transfer the funds to WREC for safekeeping
Divide the funds based on the contract terms
Return all funds to the original depositor
questions.explanation: Interpleading means the broker deposits the disputed funds with the court and asks the court to determine which party is entitled to the money. This relieves the broker of the responsibility of deciding between conflicting claims.

questions.question_text: WREC requests to examine a broker's trust account records. The broker says the records are at the accountant's office. Must the broker comply?
questions.correct_answer: Yes, records must be available at any time
distractors: No, WREC needs a court order to access
Only during a scheduled annual audit
Only if a formal complaint has been filed
questions.explanation: W.S. 33-28-122(a)(iii) obligates every responsible broker to permit the Commission or its representative to examine his trust accounting records, and WREC Rules Ch. 5 § 2 authorizes audits at the Commission's discretion — no complaint, court order, or scheduled audit is required. Failing to produce a record in the broker's possession or control concerning a transaction under investigation is itself a disciplinary ground under W.S. 33-28-111(a)(xii), and Ch. 5 § 1(e)(vi) requires the recordkeeping system to be maintained at the broker's place of business.

questions.question_text: Buyer and seller deadlock over a disputed earnest money deposit and neither will sign a release. What ends the broker's duty to keep holding the funds?
questions.correct_answer: A civil action being filed, or the broker interpleading all parties
distractors: A written determination issued by WREC
The passage of 90 days from the date of the dispute
The broker's own good-faith reading of the contract
questions.explanation: W.S. 33-28-122(f) gives three exits and no others: a written release from the parties consenting to disposition, the filing of a civil action, or the broker interpleading all parties — at which point the deposit may be paid to the court. WREC issues no determinations on disputed deposits, and no waiting period lets the broker disburse unilaterally.

questions.question_text: How long must a Wyoming broker retain trust account records?
questions.correct_answer: Not less than 2 years from the last date the company participated in the transaction
distractors: For 1 year after the transaction closes
Only until the next scheduled WREC audit
For 90 days after the funds are disbursed
questions.explanation: W.S. 33-28-123 requires the responsible broker to keep a full set of records of every real estate transaction and to maintain them not less than two (2) years from the latest date on which the real estate company participated in the transaction. Separately, W.S. 33-28-122(a)(iii) requires the broker to permit the Commission to examine trust accounting records, and WREC Rules Ch. 5 § 2 authorizes audits — so the records must be both retained for the two-year minimum and produced on request.
